Why not just encrypt your data before you put it on cloud storage or send it over the wire?

That makes it very inconvenient though.

Say you need a cloud service to save your daily files (Google Drive, Dropbox, Box.net, Amazon, Microsoft....), would you really go through the hassle to manually encrypt (and then decrypt each time) each and every one of them?

If you are talking about backups, or rarely used files, yes, this is possible, but there are lots of services that would just become too inconvenient to use in this way.

A better solution would be if, say, the Dropbox client, would encrypt the files before storing them online, leaving the keys on the host machine. This might make it practical for some uses, but still impractical for others (for instance where the server is supposed to elaborate in some way this data).

Think for instance at a cloud-hosted SQL Server that keeps sensitive data... clearly you can't encrypt the data because, if you do, then you lose the ability to use queries (where clauses, order by, joins, etc). Microsoft came up with a solution in its SQL Server 2016 (i think it is still in preview) by using "column encryption", where you tell the Server which columns should be encrypted and which you don't care... with two modes: in one mode your data is encrypted, but still searchable, sortable, etc... it doesn't use a very safe encryption because the encrypted data needs to be searchable, sortable, etc but it is still better than nothing, the other mode is real encryption, but you lose the ability to work on those columns. The encryption keys are not known to the SQL Server (the client uses them to encrypt and decrypt the data on the fly). This is IMO a good solution, because even if Microsoft receives a warrant it can say "this is the data we have, it is encrypted and we don't have the keys, good luck".

The problem here is that while, so far, we have trusted who hosted our data, now we can't anymore, because, quite frankly, your government is turning into full-fascism mode...
